utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. Once again I warn you that you are still bound by the declaration you made to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Today we're going to finish your examination-in-chief. Now we will continue. I would like to remind you once again about our mutual duty towards the interpreters to make a break between question and answer so that they could do their job properly. Yesterday we finished the day with a document that was on the monitor. I think we can look at the document again. This is Exhibit 682.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have that on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You can see the document in front of you now. Do you remember seeing this document yesterday? It's an application to be admitted to the Banja Luka secondary school for internal affairs. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at page 04006946 in the B/C/S of this document -- actually, it's page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, in the English translation it's page 3. Yes, it's page 3 of a total of four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you looked at the heading of this document. It's a document by the public security station in Drnis relating to the candidate who submitted the application for the internal affairs secondary school. Could you please tell me who this information refers to. Is that the candidate whose name we saw in the previous document, and could you please read paragraphs 2 and 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from this document, from the information, that it is the person from the document we looked at before applying to be admitted to the school of the organs of internal affairs. This document states: "Since residing -- since he no longer resides in Drnis, Aleksandar's behaviour has been quite insolent. He socialises with his peers as well as those older than he is who have a tendency for stealing, harassing elderly citizens of Croatian ethnicity, and he takes the lead in this. He's quite insolent towards the SUP workers when he talks with them." He talks about injustices and so on. His father is now on a post at Zitnic. It's a person who is prone to consuming large quantities of alcohol and as such fires in town from fire-arms and creates disorder in the house and there are frequent fights and disagreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the bottom of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read what it says in the lower right-hand counter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Information checked by Nikola Vugdelija." This is the person who actually wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Looking at this document in front of us now, is Nikola Vugdelija a staff member of the Drnis public security station, based on what is on this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this document, Nikola Vugdelija is an employee of the Drnis public security station. I happen to know him personally and I know that he worked at that station even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In view of what you have read, can you tell us what his assignment was. What is he actually reporting on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: His primary task in this report was to check the information relating to the applicant interested to be admitted to the secondary school for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 6944, the last four digits on the B/C/S copy; and in the English that is page 2. Can we look at the beginning of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose document this is, what does it say in the heading?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document of the Knin SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the subject of the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is information about enrolment at the SUP secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence before the list begins actually says: "The following candidates were not admitted." Do you see the name of the candidate who was mentioned in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the name under number 8, Aleksandar Tisma, the candidate who was not admitted to the secondary school for internal affairs. It's the name under number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There is also an explanation why certain candidates were admitted and why others were not admitted. Could you please read that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 18th of August, 1993, the commission of the Ministry of Internal Affairs selected the candidates to be enrolled at the internal affairs secondary school in Banja Luka for the 1993/1994 school year. Due to a large number of applicants, those selected had the best school grades, were physically fit, had not been prosecuted, or their family members were never prosecuted either."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on these three documents that you saw, sir, can you perhaps conclude why the candidate Tisma -- excuse me, I didn't wish to mention his name, the candidate under 8 was not admitted to school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from the documents that this candidate, number 8, was not admitted to school because of the data established during the vetting conducted by organs of the internal affairs. The candidate or himself or his father do not meet the conditions required in order to be admitted to school. His conduct is not something that is suitable and does not meet the required standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You worked in the police of SAO Krajina from 1990 until the Operation Storm. So were these criteria applied throughout that whole period? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the duty of the commissions or the managers of the organisational units of MUP, of the RSK, to vet all the candidates or new employees. They had to check all the candidates interested in attending schools and training courses of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the RSK have its own education centre where police officers were trained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RSK had its training centre in Golubic where police officers were trained. These were policemen who had already completed secondary school and served their regular military term of duty. They were trained at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has already been admitted into evidence. Can we now look at exhibit 674, please, 674. Can we zoom in on the top left-hand corner so that the witness could read it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The text is not so clear, but can you tell us who drafted this text and who is it being sent to? Can you see that from the heading?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that the document was drafted at the Korenica Secretariat for Internal Affairs and it's being sent to the 17th August education centre at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the subject of this document is. Below the heading there is always the reference, the subject. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an application for enrolment to the high school for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see underneath which school actually this is. You see two lines on the screen, and it's enough. Perhaps you can read that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Find attached applications for enrolment at the internal affairs high school in Zemun."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the bottom of the document to see who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It's unclear. Can you please tell us who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a signature there in the name of Marko Dragicevic, the secretary, but it's not him who signed it. Somebody else signed it on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on all of this, can you tell us what this case is about, what is the Korenica SUP asking the education centre in Golubic 17th August to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Korenica SUP is sending in applications for enrolment at the school for internal affairs in Zemun in Serbia. They were forwarding the list to the Golubic education centre, and they are asking the Golubic training centre to include the candidates on the list for admittance to the Zemun high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of the examination-in-chief, at the beginning of your testimony, sir, you explained that -- or you stated that in early January 1991 the SAO Krajina SUP was formed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly what was one of the main tasks of the SUP secretary?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, this question's been asked and answered already a long time ago, this exact question about the tasks and -- of the secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps my colleague is right. I just wanted to create the ambiance in order to present a document, but I can withdraw the question in order to save time and just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for saving time, Mr. Milovancevic. Move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There's just a question I'd like to ask before you proceed. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I see a reference in the document to subject: "Application to enroll at the college." Now, the word that is being mentioned is "high school." I would like to know what ages would the applicants be or the students be at this college, because there is normally some distinction between college and high school. So I'd like that clarified. I normally know college to be after high school. So could the witness answer, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, high school of internal affairs is -- comes after secondary school. So in the previous system of levels, it -- the secondary school had the third and fourth degree. Some of them had the fifth level. The higher school had the sixth level, whereas the universities had the seventh level. High schools always were counted as almost -- as having completed the first two years of university. In this particular case, the candidates attending ranged from 20 to some 30 years of age. They had already started their work and were continuing their schooling as they were working. That was the practice then in many of the Ministries for Internal Affairs in other republics, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Where does college fit in in the process, or are the two words "high school" and "college" synonymous? Did you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you, Your Honour. Higher school meant the first two years of university. So if somebody who had completed this higher school, they could enroll at a university and they could enroll straight into the third year of university. And maybe there was some exams that they had to take with the permission of the dean and then they would continue with their regular university education from the third year onwards. So that was the level of the higher school or the high school. That was the policy also with various military schools, also law schools, schools of economy. They could apply to all those universities. This actually also applied throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What the Trial Chamber was really trying to get from you is whether there is a difference between college and high school. So I beg your pardon. Maybe what I should get you to do is look at the caption, the subject matter, and translate it and see if in the course of the translation there is a reference to college or high school, because we were really trying to discover whether or not there was a distinction between what you have now described as high school and how it fits in in the scheme of training as opposed to what is there on the caption, "college." So could you please look at the subject matter in the document, that caption, and if you would read it and then maybe it could be translated and we can see where the -- the difference might be, if any. Please go ahead, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The subject here is: "Application for enrolment to the higher school for internal affairs. Please find attached applications for enrolment at the higher school for internal affairs in Zemun."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Picking up on the questions asked of you by Honourable Judge Nosworthy, let me draw your attention to the end of that sentence in the introductory part: "Please find attached applications for the higher school of internal affairs in Zemun with complete documentation for the following members." What does this word "members" mean? Who are the applicants for this school? Can you explain to us based on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see from this sentence and from the words "for the following members," that the enumerated persons are already members of the organs of internal affairs, they are employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: To put it briefly, does it mean that those applying to be enrolled in the school are already employees, police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are already police officers who are already employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let me see if we had this document -- yes, this is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show on the monitor, please, document -- or, rather, Exhibit 602.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the document appears on our screens, to save time, we see in the heading that it's a document of the Ministry of the Interior on the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina on the 26th November 1991. Let us look in the heading, please, the top of the document, please, the left top corner. What I just said - and you can now see the document - is it indeed the document of the MUP of SAO Krajina dated 26th November 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It's a document of the MUP, and the date is indeed the 26th November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read para 1. What does this document contain? What are -- what is the large lettering in the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read para 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know, I hate to interrupt because I don't want to take up more time, but we're back again to the same problem. This is a document that pertains to, from what I can see, a completely separate part of the Krajina from the part where the witness was at the time. It hasn't -- you know, he's about to start reading the document. I expect, based on the questions that we've had so far today, that he's just going to start commenting and giving his own interpretation and argument about the document, but it hasn't been established that he knows anything about this before he goes into it, and I think that that should be -- that that foundation again should be laid before he just starts commenting on it. It's not relevant if he doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this objection is completely baseless. Mr. Ari Kerkkanen does not come from Yugoslavia and still he reviewed all the documents and testified that they were indeed documents of the MUP. And now with somebody who as a policeman in the SAO Krajina we are not allowed to review the document and discuss it. I don't understand this kind of objection. The document relates to the work of Mr. Martic, and the witness has said what the duties of the secretary of the Ministry of the Interior were, beginning with the 1st of January, 1992, when the SUP of SAO Krajina was established. We heard already a part of the answers, and now when I was about to move on I have to go back. Our life is really complicated by this kind of objection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The date was the 4th of January, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just briefly, there's an obvious difference between what -- between Mr. Kerkkanen's testimony and what the counsel seeks to elicit from these witnesses. Mr. Kerkkanen simply introduced the documents based on his document missions, did not comment on them except to say what they said, and then they were introduced into evidence. This document is already into evidence. It's available to the Trial Chamber. It's available to Defence counsel to argue about later. What we don't have here is any basis, and I don't believe that Defence counsel has supplied a basis in his response, for believing that this witness can shed any additional light on the document, aside from what's there before our eyes. And this is just a -- you know, a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just like yesterday, I think the question is lay a basis for what you want to say -- what do you want this witness to say about this document. Because we can read what is on this document and we don't need to have this witness interpret unless you have laid the base -- basis for his interpretation that you want from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence believes that the witness has already provided a basis for this question. He spoke in general terms about the work of the secretariat of internal affairs, that is the MUP of SAO Krajina. And our intention is not for the -- to have the witness comment upon this individual document, but to use this document as a basis for telling us his position, whether this was a common phenomenon or just an individual-only case. So we are interested in the whole phenomenon and it's -- the frequency of its occurrence. And we believe that the witness, in view of his line of work and his experience, can give an answer that would be of assistance and -- to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What phenomenon do you want to establish, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The general phenomenon, the general need in the period when the SUP of SAO Krajina was being created to establish police stations with the war and secession, the existing order was totally broken up, although there were -- there was personnel, there was -- there were police stations, there were secretariats. But the legal system stopped functioning. Financing stopped. Military occupation, a siege occurred. And now I want to elicit from the witness, using this document as an illustration, to tell us whether this was a lonely instance or something that occurred generally. That's all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, but then -- but then that explanation -- then it becomes a leading approach to this witness. He's going to show the witness a phenomenon and then say: Well, did this occur elsewhere? Why doesn't he just ask what occurred and what the witness knows without using the document in that way. So either he lays a foundation for it and then uses the document or he just asks the witness what he knows. But to kind to confuse the two processes I don't think is proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you say you want to find out whether this kind of order was a general order given all over the country, all over the SAO Krajina. Let me just understand what it is you say you want to do with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not really in that sense, not literally. I think that I can use this -- it's not that I want to use this document as something that applies to the entire SAO Krajina, but I was going to ask whether this document speaks of a phenomenon that either did or didn't exist in the territory of Krajina from what he knows and from what he has experienced in various parts of that territory and in various police stations. That was the purport of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is all you want to establish? In that instance, I'll let you ask the question. Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read to us para 1 of this order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In keeping with the verbal and written agreement with the commander of the Banja Luka Corps, Lieutenant-General Nikola Ozelac [phoen], to the effect that the affairs covered by civilian authorities in war-time conditions in the area of Dubica and Kostajnica, pending the establishment of police stations in Dubica, all these affairs relating to public security in the local commune of Dubica will be performed -- will be covered by the public security station of Kostajnica with the help of the military police, the Banja Luka Corps, or more precisely the 3rd Detachment."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at para 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read it for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All persons wearing camouflage uniforms, while not being members of the police of the SAO Krajina, while not having appropriate IDs of authorised officers, or while not having been legally appointed by the Ministry of the Interior of Krajina, are required to return all insignia of the police and report to the military department of Kostajnica in order to be included in the wartime formations of the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is the signatory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this document, I want to ask you this about the problem of establishing police stations in certain areas and restoring order in terms of unauthorised wearing of police uniforms. Did this problem exist only in the area of Kostajnica or did it exist elsewhere as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please don't preach to the witness before you ask your questions. Just ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, and get to that question you said you wanted to ask about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The question is -- the question is, Witness: In 1991, did the MUP of SAO Krajina set up police stations in areas where they did not exist before and did the MUP of SAO Krajina have any problems with maintaining law and order as far as unauthorised wearing of uniforms is concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, when there were combat operations all over Krajina, the legal and territorial divisions between municipalities that existed before were disrupted so that certain areas were left without any police stations and were no longer covered by police personnel, and a kind of vacuum emerged. It was not clear at the beginning which authorities from which territory had jurisdiction in terms of police work. Many problems occurred, and after a certain time smaller police stations, police sections, and outposts were established, including larger public security stations. I remember the instance of Drnis, where after combat activities in 1991, all the personnel of the public security station of Drnis left the area because they were all Croats and they were at that station after that mutiny in 1991. So a year later they left the station, they left the town and the entire area, and the area remained without any police. And all the problems that existed before remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but I thought, in essence, two questions had been asked rolled up in one. The first relating to the MUP of the SAO K and whether police stations were set up in areas where they didn't exist before; and then a second question was concerning problems with the wearing or unauthorised wearing of uniforms. Has the question been -- well, maybe you could separate the questions because that may well have been what confused the witness. And if that was what you wanted to get from the witness, those two questions, we could get him to be focussed in his answers. I remind him from yesterday, less is more. And if he could just please answer directly. Mr. Milovancevic, I think you will have to try and guide him because there are time constraints also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I hate to rise, but I think that second question that the Chamber identified, which was, yes, contained in Mr. Milovancevic's question, I think that was asked and answered yesterday. I think that was addressed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I thought it was addressed yesterday, but I didn't know whether there was something more that he had wanted from the witness that could assist us in the area. But I do agree with you, I recall that that question was placed on the record yesterday and dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard the suggestion by Her Honour Judge Nosworthy. You've responded to the first part of the question. The second part of the question related to the authorised or unauthorised wearing of the uniform. You did talk about that yesterday. Can you tell us whether the Ministry of Internal Affairs intervened if it found out about such instances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did intervene --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just a short answer: Yes, they did; or no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat your answer. Did you intervene or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we would intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Responding to one of my questions yesterday, you explained that the Secretariats of Internal Affairs -- or, rather, public security stations had to report back to superior. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were obliged to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at a document on the 65 ter list that bears the number 701.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we see the document, so as not to lose any time, this is a document with a title compulsory instruction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are asked to slow down, Mr. Milovancevic, when you're reading so that the interpreters can keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we can look at the top of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this instruction, whose title I read out? It's a long title.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It's in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a moment, can we look at page 10 in the B/C/S of this document; in the English translation, that is page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read item 32 and underneath that can you look at the date of the document and see who drafted the document. Can you see that on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read item 32, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no 32 on my page. It is on page 16 of my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's page 15, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's -- sorry. It's at page 14. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my translation, Your Honours, page 14 ends with article 30 of the instruction. Article 32 is on page 15 that I asked the witness to read. And then there is only one line on page 16. So perhaps we have the different layout as far as the translation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please read item 32.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the day this instruction goes into effect, the instruction on reporting in public security tasks and other tasks of internal affairs ceases to be in force. Number 11-021-10/74, dated the 3rd of June, 1974. This compulsory instruction is dated the 20th of May, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the very bottom of the document. We can't see now who the signatory of the document is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that the document was signed by Minister Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 1 of this document, where you can see articles 2 and 3. The last two -- the last three numbers in the B/C/S are 917, if that makes it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read article 2 of these instructions. What does it say regarding the duty to inform?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, we do not have the translation of English in front of us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters say that don't have a translation before them, so will you please slow down so they can interpret properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please read slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Item 2. Organs of internal affairs are duty-bound in a timely manner and completely to report and inform on the state of security on occurrences and events from the internal affairs sphere as well as on measures and activities they are carrying out in accordance with their legal authorisations and duties. Besides mutual reporting and informing, organs of internal affairs are to regularly inform the Assemblies of socio-political and regional communities and the leaderships of socio-political organisations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that the internal affairs organs were duty-bound to do this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of that and we acted in accordance with these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at item 4 of this document, please. This is page 2 in the B/C/S, and in the English translation it's also page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read article 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Information implies gathering data, notices, other information, their selection and classification, as well as compiling daily and extraordinary information on events and occurrences in order to inform the authorised organs and leaderships about the state of security in a certain area."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been shown a document before informing about the situation in the Benkovac security station from the 10th to the 24th of December, and it also mentions an incident that happened in that period. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This document, in your opinion, does it contain the information as it is listed in item 4 here of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that we looked at a day or two ago here was drafted on the basis of this instruction and contains most of the information required according to item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please read articles 6 and 7 of this document. They are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we can scroll up a little bit -- scroll down a little bit. On the English translation that is page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The organisational unit of the joint Secretariat for Internal Affairs, from here on joint secretariat, is obliged to inform the organ of internal affairs on all events and occurrences, as provided for with this instruction, immediately opinion learning of the event or occurrence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you read item 7 which also refers to the organisational unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Organisational unit of the joint secretariat, on the basis of gathered and received data and information, during a period of 24 hours, until the beginning of work hours, drafts a daily report on the situation and events in its region that are of importance for engaging workers and for their activities and should inform the authorised officials in the organisational unit and the joint secretariat."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spent a certain amount of time at the public security station in Benkovac. Did that station inform the higher instance, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did report to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Was that in accordance with this instruction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was in accordance with this instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at article or item 9 of this document. It's page 3 in the B/C/S and in English it's on page 4. Item 9 is at the very top of this page. Can we look at that, please. Can you -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you read item 9 of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All more important events, occurrences, and measures taken should be urgently passed on by the internal affairs organ to the Ministry of Internal Affairs."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked about the organs within the Ministry of Internal Affairs starting from police stations, then public security stations, SUPs, all the way up to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you have information whether this duty to report on all things happening in the field was in force? Did that exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the duty to report on all undertaken actions and measures, and I can say that we did fulfil this obligation. I'm not aware that there were any organisational units that did not carry out their reporting duties because this was something that they were obliged to do; and if this was not done, then the person in charge would have to deal with that immediately in order to resolve that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning when we first looked at this document you read out item 32, which states that on the day that this instruction goes into effect, the instruction on reporting is no longer in effect. This is the previous instruction that was in force in the old Yugoslavia, which went into effect in 1974. Do you remember whether this instruction contained some provisions, such as this one that relate to reporting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the instruction from 1974 also contained such provisions and that most of this material is practically identical, it's similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what, in your opinion, was the objective of this instruction. What is the sense, what is the purpose of its existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, this instruction aims to ensure that the leadership of higher or larger organisational units is informed about the situation in the field, which measures were being taken, so that the superior organs can monitor events and the activities and conduct of internal affairs staff out in the field. So the leadership was supervising what the subordinates were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And respecting this instruction, did that contribute to maintaining law and order or not? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The existence of this instruction did improve the work of internal affairs organs and contributed to better control over lower-ranking stations. Thus, it improved the work of all sectors of internal affairs and in all assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number? Mr. Milovancevic, while we are at this point, can I ask you how much longer are you going to be? You estimated seven hours for this witness, and you have gone far beyond seven hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe another 15 minutes. I just have another two documents to go through. I'm very close to the end, and I'll try to use my time as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we must talk about what you plan to do because you have taken the entire seven hours alone and more, which seven hours we had cut down to four.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think actually we're about at ten hours now, over ten hours of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are over ten hours. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become exhibit number 893.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In response to the Defence's questions you said the police wore uniforms. Did they also wear insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were required to wear emblems of rank and position on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at a Prosecution document from the 65 ter list number 748. This document is entitled "rules of procedure concerning emblems of rank, position, and the uniforms of authorised officers of the organs of internal affairs."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this title?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please turn to page 7 in B/C/S, and that would be page 10 in English, just to see when this document originated. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You can see the date and the author.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was created on the 22nd of June, 1993, and the author is Minister Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to the front page and then look at page 2, which is also 2 in English. Article 2 is at the very bottom of this page. Can we look at the bottom of this first page? That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In article 2 it is stipulated that for certain positions or titles, certain insignia are prescribed. Some of them are described on this page and others on page 2 in B/C/S. To save time, I will put to you the various titles that police officers had in SAO Krajina. One of them is junior policeman, then policeman of first class, senior policeman, and all the way to independent inspector, senior inspector, senior inspector first class, and chief inspector. I want to ask you: Are you aware that these titles existed in the Ministry of the Interior? Of course I mean the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These titles did exist in the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Krajina, but the titles from junior police officers to the senior officer first class are those of authorised officers with secondary education, whereas the ones above senior inspector first class up to the chief inspector required a degree, a university degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move on to page 4 in B/C/S, which is 7 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Here under the subheading "uniform" we see article 6 describing the summer uniform for the MUP of Serbian Krajina, and it says: "Cap, beret, shirt, trousers with belt, and light shirt." It goes on to say that there is an Nemanjic coat of arms on the beret and a wind-breaker, as well as the emblem or patch with the lettering "Milicija Krajina," police of Krajina, for the left sleeve. It says that the camouflage uniform is of a dark colour, and it says: "When performing special assignments or missions, authorised officers may use fatigues as a uniform of a dark blue camouflage design." Are you aware that the camouflage uniform for the police of Krajina was precisely like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at page 6 of this document in B/C/S; in English it would be page 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Those are transitional and final provisions. It says: "Emblems of title and rank worn by authorised officers in keeping with the descriptions above shall be replaced with emblems of title and rank, as stipulated in these rules of procedure." My question is: Until the entry into force of these rules, did there exist another document that stipulated the uniforms, the titles, and rank insignia for members of the MUP of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before we used to have a set of rules regulating these matters and we complied with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at our last document and that will be the end of your examination-in-chief. It's Exhibit 511. The title of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may be of assistance. I don't believe that that last document was admitted into evidence, and we would certainly consent to it being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my learned friend. I thought it was already an exhibit and it isn't. May I tender it now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 894.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You now see a Prosecution document bearing the title "list of staff members of the SUP of Knin who entered into employment for an indefinite period of time from 1990 to date." To find our way more easily through this document, documents are arranged by months, but in inverse order starting from December 1992 down to 1990. It's perhaps not the best kind of order, but the document could not be shown differently than in the form in which we received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 5198. The first page is 5197, the following one is 5198, and in English it's page 2. Can we just see the middle of this text. Here. Thank you. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, above this set of three names we see some numbers. Can you read that for us, please, Witness. Does it say 11/92 and 12/92?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see 11/92 and 12/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Below each of these there is a set of names, and next to each name there is a date. Let me remind you this is a list of employees who were admitted into employment, and that must be the date when they were employed. In the first group, all the dates were from November 1992, and in the second set all the dates were from December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 5216. In English it's page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just -- I think this shouldn't be broadcast. I don't know if it's being broadcast by the booth, but the document should not by broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you. Should we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe we should do that after the break, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll be done in five minutes, Your Honour. Let us take the break now and after the break I'll finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask you to move into private session for a moment because of the document I'm intending to present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the document we've just seen, can you tell us whether the list refers to the period when you transferred to the public security station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that period as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 5212 in B/C/S. That is a list of employees who signed employment contracts between the 1st of January, 1991 until the 31st of December, 1991. In English it's 19 to 25, beginning with page 19 until 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You see before you a list of employees whose employment contracts date back to January, the 1st of January, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It has several pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the bottom of the page to see how many people there are on the list? Thank you. Can we turn the page now, see the next page in B/C/S. This page is all right as well. We are now on page 4 of the document. Let us see the bottom of the page to see how many employees are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is the last number you see on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the person under 147?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petar Veselinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in English this is on page 21 because the pages are not exactly in the proper order. That's the way they were typed. So on page 21 you should be able to see the end of this document showing that the last number is 147. Have you found it, Your Honours? I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to this document, how many people began working full time on -- in January 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1991, 147 workers started to work for an indefinite period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the previous composition of the police station, is this a large increase?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This number, yes, would constitute an increase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why such a large number of people came to the public security station in Knin. Do you have any information about that? Were these policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people came to the Knin SUP. They were all authorised officials from towns on the Croatian coast or from Zagreb or from other towns where the Krajina authorities were not in charge, and according to what they said they could no longer live there and work there so they came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just tell us why, not where they came from. We haven't got much time now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came because they felt that they could no longer work in those towns and live there. They were in danger. They were harassed, so they crossed into the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last question that I'm going to put to you, Witness, is the following. You were a member of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs in the 1990-1995 period when the RSK was in existence. In that period of time, did you manage to see any kind of parallel system of authority which would be in competition with yours and which threatened you? Can you please answer with yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I believe we're in private session still, and we can go into public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, we are in public session. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me introduce myself. My name is Alex Whiting. You obviously have figured out in the days that you've been here that I'm one of the Prosecutors in the case. I hope you don't mind me saying that I notice that sometimes you give rather lengthy answers, and I'm going to ask when -- in response to my questions that you try, please, very much to focus on the question that I'm asking and answer only the question that I'm asking. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. But in order to clarify the situation for all of us, in order to fulfil the goal of my testimony here, sometimes I believe that I need to give a slightly more -- broader answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we need a broader answer, the Prosecutor will ask for a broader answer. Just answer the question that he asks and stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just want to warn you, I won't be shy about interrupting you. Now, sir, you testified on the very first day that you were here that 90 per cent of the inhabitants of the Knin municipality were Serbs and that the head of the police in that area would usually be a Serb and his deputy would be a Croat. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I take it from that, from what you testified to, that there's a connection between those two facts. The -- a Serb was designated as the chief of the -- of the police in the Knin municipality because the municipality was comprised of 90 per cent Serbs. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that from what you knew that it is certain - and you used the word "certain" - that there were more Croats on the police force than Serbs. That's at 6724. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, the question is not clear to me that there were more Croats than Serbs. I either made a slip of the tongue or there's a mistake in the transcript. I said that at that time there were more Serbs than Croats at the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There was a confusion there. I'm not talking about the Knin police station; I'm talking about in all of Croatia. You were answering a question about the composition of the police in all of Croatia, and you testified that you were certain that there were more Croat policemen in Croatia than Serb policemen. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. Now it's clear that you meant the whole of Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, you are certain of that fact. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, sir. I didn't ask you if you were -- think that's how it was. I asked you are you were certain of that fact as you sit here today. You used that word in direct examination. Are you certain of that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, isn't it true that Serbs made up at least 60 per cent of the police force in Croatia at that time? Isn't that the fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that fact, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you a segment of an interview with the accused, Milan Martic, which he gave when he was president of the RSK in October of 1994. It's in evidence as Exhibit 497.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask that we -- is there -- I'm going to ask that we switch over to the Sanction to watch this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, having seen now Mr. Martic talking about this subject, do you accept that you are wrong and that in fact Serbs made up 60 per cent of the police force in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where Mr. Martic got this information from, but if you have the official information about percentage of 60 -- 60 per cent of Serbs in the MUP at that time in Croatia, I will accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, sir. My question is: Now that you've seen Mr. Martic speak about it, are you still certain about what you testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would stand by what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another document. I'm going to show you a report from Human Rights Watch which reported the figures from the Croatian government. And it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If it could be called up on the e-court. It's 00276596. I hope that's sufficient to -- I don't believe we have a -- a translation in B/C/S of this document, but I'm just going to rely on a sentence here. If we could go to page 23 of the document. And if we could go to the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In that first full paragraph, the third sentence says, and I'll just read it slowly. It says: "According to the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, Serbs accounted for approximately 75 per cent of the Croatian police force, despite the fact that they comprised only 11.5 per cent of the republic's population." Okay, now that you've seen Mr. Martic's view of the figures and you've seen a report about the Croatian Ministry of Interior's view, do you question your own information, that the Croats made -- were -- there were more Croats in the police department -- in the police in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that it would be useful also if the Prosecutor were to tell the witness the date of the report itself and to which period this information relates to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought this document relates to the period during the communist era. It says: "During the communist era a vast majority of the police officers in Croatia were Serbian." I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, to be fair, I didn't read that sentence to the witness so he couldn't be aware of that. But yes, the document is dated September 1991, but this is about the communist era, presumably 1990 and before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now that you have that information, sir, do you think that perhaps you were wrong in -- in your own information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I see this document it's not clear to me -- you say that it refers to the communist period, that is also 1946, 1950, and 1990. I was talking about 1990, the beginning of the events in the Knin Krajina, and then knowing the situation at the place where I worked, which was a large body. And if I were to use that as a sample in order to analyse the entire composition in Croatia, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you for a moment. I'm sorry. The document I've shown you is not about 1946/1950. This is a document about the events in Croatia in 1990/1991. So I put to you that the figure there of 75 per cent is pertaining to 1990 and before. Now, does the information that I have put to you cause you in any way to question your own information about whether Croats or Serbs were the majority in the police in Croatia, or are you still, having seen all this, certain about what you testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This report that is in English, and seeing that it was comprised by Slavko Degoricija and Milan Brezak, this report is something that I do not consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, please answer the question. We don't need your comment on this report. Just say whether you stand by your answer or you don't stand by your answer. That's -- the question is simple and straightforward.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, given Mr. Martic's position within the SAO Krajina police and the RSK, don't you think that he would have better information on these topics than you did, or that you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he could not have had better information, if we're looking at 1990. I had better information because I was in touch with the top leadership of the ministry of the Republic of Croatia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the date of that clip that we saw a couple of minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's -- the interview was given on October of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, so are you saying then that when you gave the figure of -- that Croats were -- there were more Croats in the police within Croatia than Serbs, that you were relying on figures provided by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia at the time? Is that what I understand from your last answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't provide that data. This was confidential information. I concluded that from --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, please, tell me how it is you concluded that information. What are you basing it on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My information is based on my work in years before that, on many years that I worked at a certain body in Croatia, and also on the basis of analysis during my school days when we were undergoing training, based on the structure of my class and similar classes while I was attending police training school in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in other words, you extrapolated based on your classes how many Croats versus how many Serbs were in the Croatian police department? That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the indicators at the time was that we were completing our education together, and I knew who was who. We were in a pretty equal situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going to have to learn to answer the question. The question to you is: Did you extrapolate that from your classes on how many Croats versus how many Serbs there were in the Croatian police department? The answer to that question is either a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, based on that personal analysis derived from your classes, you told this Trial Chamber that you were certain of your information and you stand by that information now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to find out something. When -- what year were you told that in your class?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I attended the school in Zagreb from 1979 to -- from 1977 to 1979.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is: In what year were you told that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. What was I told?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were going to school from 1977 to 1979. When you got this information about the numbers of police in the force, was it in 1977, in 1978, in 1979, in any one of those three years? Which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was attending school, there were other students attending with me. So on the basis of who was what, who belonged to which ethnic group, I knew more or less how many Serbs there were, how many Croats were. On the basis of that experience as well as on the basis of my work experience, I conclude that -- or I concluded that the number of Serbs and Croats working in the MUP was more or less equal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's your answer now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, during 1990 and 1991 you accept, do you not, that the Croatian government was expanding the police force in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that in your view the security situation had not deteriorated to the extent that new police were required, but you also testified several times that as early as 1990 there were increased tensions. You talked about major disorder in Benkovac that occurred in March of 1990. You talked about a rally in Split that caused great anxiety. Given those tensions and difficulties that were arising, isn't it unsurprising that Croatia was expanding its police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of the police was regularly changing. Constantly new people were joining the force. But such a change in numbers and including more Croats in the police force, was something that was hard to understand. And in my opinion, it was unjustified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Even given the tensions and disorders that you -- you yourself testified about, and you talked about your own position that you assumed in July 1990, that it carried with it a lot of responsibility and that there was a lot of tension in the area. Even given all that testimony that you have provided to this Trial Chamber, you still maintain that it was hard to understand that Croatia would expand its police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, at the time, if there was a need to employ new workers, this was not something that called for very high numbers, but this was not something that should have been done in the way that the Croatian MUP was doing it, the way it was engaging new staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So now your answer is that new staff was justified but not so many and not in the way that it was done. Is that now your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, in the position that you assumed in July 1990, it's fair to say, isn't it, that you were trusted by your superiors. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: However, you testified on several occasions that you were distrusted by some citizens of Knin because even though you were a Serb they thought that you had been brought to Knin on behalf of the Croatian authorities and that you were in fact a spy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that you were distrusted simply because you were associated in these people's minds with the Croatian authorities. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact -- and I'm going to take a brief diversion here. You testified that you were called an Ustasha simply because you had tried to calm a crowd on August 17th, 1990 that had gathered in anger over Martic's suspension. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to answer just with yes or no, then I will not really be able to provide the true answers because to me it seems more to be a leading question. Because if you permit me, Your Honours, to at least explain a little bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please, I'm going to interrupt you, sir, because -- and I understand that you're -- you may not be familiar with the system, but I get to ask leading questions. That's my job in these proceedings. It's different from when Defence counsel's asking you questions. So, yes, it's a leading question. Now, if you could just yes or no, you were called -- and I can read your testimony if you like, and then if you want to provide a brief explanation I'll permit you to do that. But yes or no, you were called an Ustasha, weren't you, in August of 1990 by the crowd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I think it would be prudent to redact that last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if I can remind you, please, to take care, as best you can, not to refer to your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May that answer, starting at page 44, lines 12 to 22, please be deleted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, I wasn't really asking about that. What I was asking about is the -- what I was focussing in on is the fact that you were called an Ustasha. Now, you were not an Ustasha, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, not then and not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you would agree with me, I take it, that that term "Ustasha" is a pretty -- was a pretty inflammatory term at the time. You would agree with me, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you would agree with me also that based on your personal experience that this term was obviously used to describe people who were not in fact Ustashas. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that when Serb leaders described the Croatian government again and again and again as an Ustasha government, that that made the Serb people afraid, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that time when Mr. Raskovic made public appearances and he divided in his speeches the Croat people into good Croats and into bad Croats, whom he called Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to my question, sir. When the leaders, the Serb leaders, in the Krajina, Mr. Raskovic, Mr. Babic, Mr. Martic, when they described the government of Croatia as an Ustasha government, that made Serbs afraid, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of their motivation for calling the Croatian government --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, sir. I didn't ask you about the motivation. I did not ask you anything about the motivation. I asked you about the effect that it had on the Serbian people. They're being told by their leaders that the government of Croatia is an Ustasha government. That made them afraid, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that caused fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony you said -- you testified that before the first multi-party elections in 1990 that -- and I'm going to quote from your testimony here. You said: "All the parties that were founded were, for the most part, nationalist parties and their rallies were -- had a sort of nationalist tone. All of them propagated being freed or liberated from something." And that's at 6719. Now, you talked -- you then went on to talk about the HDZ, but that was also true of the principal party on the Serb side, the SDS, wasn't it? It was also a nationalist party; wouldn't you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, let's get back to the situation in Knin in July of 1990, and you've told us that you were distrusted by some of the people in Knin and you gave an explanation for why that was. Now, isn't it a fact that you were also distrusted by -- for some of the same reasons by some of the Serb officers within the police in Knin? Isn't that also true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, although we never discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking if it's possible. You know it to be true, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know. I never discussed it. I never discussed whether anybody trusted me or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's look at a prior statement that you made to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'd ask the assistance of the usher to provide this statement to the witness and to the Trial Chamber. I'm going to use it in hard copy. I think it's much easier than trying to put it on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
