utterances.text: Sir, do you have a copy of this statement in your own language before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you -- do you also have the English version?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at page 10 of the English version. There is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, because you have protective measures, we redacted your -- the name on the last page. So I'm going to have to give you -- for this purpose, I'm going to have to give you an unredacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if I could again have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could look at the last page, page 10 of the English, it's called "witness acknowledgement." And in English it says: "This statement has been read over to me in the Serbian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." And is that your signature there? And don't say the name, but is that your signature there dated 18 September 2000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to go into private session for this purpose, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, isn't it fair to say that the distrust also went the other way. You did not completely trust those policemen in Knin who had signed the petition in July of 1990, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what you mean when you say I didn't trust them. My attitude to them was the same as to all other employees of the station, and you could see that that was my approach from the way I gave them assignments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Stay on the question. You should know whether you did or did not distrust them, irrespective of what your attitude towards them may have been. Just answer the question. Did you or did you not distrust some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be precise, I did not have absolute trust in anybody. I was cautious with every employee of the Knin SUP when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why then does it take you several questions before you answer? Why don't you answer these questions the first time they're asked honestly? You said: "To be precise, I did not have absolute trust ..." Why do you become precise only after several questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the honourable Prosecutor asks me a question, he usually seeks a yes or no answer. But these matters are not black and white.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is a very straightforward one. The question had been: You did not trust some of the police that had signed the petition. And your answer was: I don't know what you mean. What is the difficulty in that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult because the question was phrased: You did not trust some of them. I said that I did not trust anybody, at least not absolutely, and I was very cautious in my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the first time you should have said: In fact, I mistrusted all of them. But to say: I don't know what you mean, what is it that you didn't understand in that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the reference to "some of them." Who was meant? There was several different groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nobody explained to you what "some of them" meant. How did you then finally come to say: To be precise, I did not trust all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know anyone at that Knin police station when I arrived, and some problems had begun before with assigning of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is simply: Nobody explained to you what the word "some" means. How then do you finally come to say: No, actually, it's not some, it's all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I mistrusted everyone in that police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. My question is: How then do you understand the word "some" without it being explained to you? To be able to know that in fact it is not some that you mistrusted but all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when the Prosecutor asked me: Isn't it true that you didn't trust some people, I didn't understand what kind of trust he meant, whether it concerned my job or some parts of my job. But the truth is I didn't trust anyone, at least not absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He didn't ask -- he didn't say "some people," he said "some members of the police in Knin" and specified them specifically, those who signed the petition. You knew exactly what he was talking about, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand him at that moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which moment did you understand him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later, when I started giving a broader answer and when we started narrowing things down and clarifying, then I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which broader answer did you give that made you understand and where was the narrowing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I started talking about the time when I arrived, the situation I found there at the station, the earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... he's just asked you about the mistrust of the police who signed the petition, and since then he hasn't talked about the time when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know what to say anymore. What do you want me to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you say what you want to say, but please answer my questions. My question to you from the beginning which caused this whole discussion between you and I was -- or in fact it was a statement -- no, it was a question: Why does it take you several questions to answer a question? Why don't you answer questions directly. That was my question. And you gave all these sorts of explanations. Now you say you don't know what explanations to give. I guess you also don't know what explanations you have been giving me. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I wish to give a precise answer, I also provide a broader context so that you can understand the situation. From now on, I will give shorter and narrower answers, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what we've been asking you to do. And just answer questions and don't try to hide by saying you don't understand words that are obviously known to you. You do know what the word "some" means, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do know what "some" means, don't you? The answer is either yes or no. You said you were going to give short answers. Give me a short answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've now testified that you had some distrust of all the members of the police department, but that's not true, is it? You told us yourself that when you received the order from Sibenik to seize the reserve weapons of Knin, that you asked the assistance of several of the employees who had not signed the petition. That appears at 6759. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that is in distinction -- that was different from other -- other assignments. For example, the -- you had testified about the assignment at Srb in July of 1990, and there you said that you picked --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend from the Prosecution quoted a part of the witness's statement, and I don't know if he quoted it very precisely. The witness spoke about matching one employee who did sign that petition with another who didn't, sending them to one and the same assignment. And he also said that he treated all his underlings equally. Could my learned friend show us exactly that passage in the statement that shows that he was looking precisely for an employee who had not signed the petition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I cited it in my question. It's at 6759. And when I read the question, I was quoting from the testimony of the witness, and the witness in fact confirmed that this was his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you still have a question -- an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, that was different -- you did it different -- you did things differently with that assignment than with previous assignments; for example, the assignment regarding the Serb National Council in Srb. There, as I think Defence counsel was referring to, you picked half individuals who had signed the petition and half who had not. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get an answer. Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He's waiting for the translation maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you -- sir, did you hear the question? Did you understand the question? The question is that on previous assignments you did it differently. You assigned members who had signed the petition along with members who had not signed the petition. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the sound of interpretation I was getting was interrupted and then I got a repeated question. Could the Prosecutor give me the question again briefly because I want to give a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe just quote that 67 and deal with that before you deal with the -- of removing that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning of this line of questioning, and it's at 6759 of the transcript, that when you received the order from Sibenik to seize the reserve weapons of Knin you asked "the assistance of several of the employees who had not signed that petition back then." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that part of my testimony. Let me just say that on that occasion I asked the assistance of one man and only in accordance with the orders and recommendation of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to remind you of the instruction from the Trial Chamber. Please just answer the question -- you fully answered that question when you said: "I remember that part of my testimony," and the explanation was unnecessary to respond to the question, okay? And your job as a witness here is simply to respond to the questions, not to argue or try to provide context. Just please respond to the questions. Now, the approach that you described there at -- relying on the assistance of -- and you said: "Several of the employees who had not signed the petition back then," that was different from the approach that you had taken on prior occasions when in fact you used half people who had signed the petition and half people who had not signed the petition. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the reason you took a different approach in August of 1990 with respect to seizing the weapons from Knin is that for that assignment you could not fully trust those members of the police who had signed the petition. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also testified that there was a petition circulating around Knin with the names of the eight policemen who did not sign the petition. Do you remember that testimony? It's at 6741.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that petition was designed, was it not, to put pressure on those policemen to sign the petition, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, you told us that -- and this is at 6801, that these officers nearly got killed, nearly got lynched, in the days after August 17th, and that they had to escape out of the back-door of the police station. Isn't that right? Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember not all eight of them were at the station. There was some of them, yes, that is correct, and it's correct that they had to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, given what we have just been talking about, about the fact that there were members of the police in Knin who did not trust you and that you did not completely trust the members of the police department yourself, would you accept the possibility that you were not informed about everything that was going on in the police department at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I can't definitely say that it was so, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you accept the -- that possibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you learn, for example, when you arrived in July of 1990 that Milan Martic had been secretly preparing the Serb policemen in Knin in fight the Croatian authorities from as early as January or February of 1990? Did you learn that fact when you arrived or were you not informed of that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't informed, and this is the first time that I am hearing that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play for you another clip from the interview that Mr. Martic gave in October of 1994, and again this was -- he gave this interview while he was president of the RSK. This is in evidence as Exhibit 497.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could switch to the Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I'll put to you -- I'm not going to play -- I wanted to just play a short clip, but I'll put to you that this refers in the interview to the period of January 1990. It's the first half of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could play that clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, now that you've seen that clip --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just for the purposes of the record it's on page 3 of the -- that clip is from page 3 of the transcript which is in evidence of -- in Exhibit 497.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now that you've seen that clip, do you accept that this was happening and that you were not aware of it, that Mr. Martic was organising the police and that it was something that you were not aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what he says, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is a convenient time for the break. Thank you, Your Honour. I believe. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I've got a minute, but I'm about to start another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break now and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when you came to the Knin police department in July of 1990, were you informed that a couple weeks before, around the 5th of July of 1990, that some high-level Croatian officials, including the Minister of Interior, Josip Boljkovic, and also his associate, and also Ante Bujas from Sibenik had come to Knin to meet and negotiate with Milan Martic and the other Serb policemen who had signed that petition? Were you made aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at least that's the interpretation I heard, the minister of internal affairs is Josip Boljkovac not Boljkovic. I wasn't following the English, so I don't know what my learned friend from the Prosecution said, but I just wanted to make sure that the correction is put in now and not later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. He said the minister was Boljkovac not Boljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I meant to say Boljkovac but it's very possible that I mispronounced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you now understand who we are talking about, Witness? We are talking about Boljkovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, I understand, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now with that clarification, were you made aware that this meeting had taken place around the 5th of July, 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you made aware of the fact that the Croat authorities required the protection of the Serb policemen in order to leave the meeting unharmed? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that from the -- at least from the point of view or from the perspective of the policemen who had signed the petition, which was as you told us all but eight of the policemen in Knin, that they believed after that meeting that the Croat authorities had no real authority anymore in Knin. Did you know that? Were you told that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you another clip. It's from the same interview. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just for the record, it appears on page 13 of the transcript of the interview, which is Exhibit 497. And if we could switch to the Sanction, please, for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you weren't told those things that Mr. Martic just said when you arrived in Knin in July of 1990, around the 12th or 13th of July, you weren't told about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. You fully answered that question when you said the word "no." And the additional explanation about another event is not required. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is there a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Hoepfel was suggesting we delete that answer -- that part of the answer which you don't want where he -- where the witness refers to his position as ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I'm very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we redact that line, that is page 61, line 12 to 13, except the "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, would you accept that in fact you did not know everything that was happening in the Knin public security station in -- at that time when you were there? Would you accept that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's more than just possible, isn't it, sir? Having seen how Mr. Martic -- unless you believe that Mr. Martic isn't telling the truth or is making it up. Having seen how Mr. Martic talked about that time period and having told us what you knew and what you didn't know, would you accept now that you did not know everything that was happening in the Knin police department at the time you were there in July of 1990?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, sorry, did you not just say that the witness arrived in Knin a week after, around a week after that meeting? So that your question would refer to the days before his arrival?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I'm grateful, Your Honour. I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put the question to you a little bit more broadly. At that time when you arrived, in the days -- would you accept that you were not aware of everything that had happened before your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of the events before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified that in connection with the events in August of 1991, that some days after August 17th that Milan Martic said and that -- and it was -- I believe it was televised that "as long as he was in charge of the police, the chequer-board would never get in Knin." This appears at 6802. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you aware -- were you made aware of the fact that he said very similar words, almost identical to that, the day of or the day after the meeting with the Croatian authorities on July 5th of 1990? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor in his previous question mentioned the page number but did not quote the statement. And now he's paraphrasing a speech. So it would be important to have the actual sentence from the witness's response. I'm just following the instructions that have been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Aren't you finding the speech at the page that he cited, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. I did quote it word for word from that page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except that in your quotation you said "he"; you didn't say "I."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's because I was quoting. That's because I was quoting. I was being faithful to the text. In the text the way the witness said it is -- the witness was quoting Milan Martic who said as long as he, Milan Martic, was in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. You are quoting the witness, you are not quoting Milan Martic. Okay. That's fine. The quotation is not a paraphrase according to Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the time Martic was not at the head of the police at all. We saw a video clip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the issue. The issue is the Prosecutor is quoting the witness where the witness said: "As long as I am" -- where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood, Your Honour. I understand what you are telling me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- in charge."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness's statement is being quoted, not a statement by Mr. Martic. Now I understand. I'm sorry. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But to be clear, the witness in that statement was quoting Milan Martic, so ultimately it is a statement by Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, sir, that -- were you made aware when you arrived in the police station in July of 1990 that Mr. Martic had made a very similar statement about the chequer-board never flying in Knin? I believe there was a reference to the fort, it would never fly over the fort, that he made that statement around July 5th of 1990? Are you aware -- were you made aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to now move to some events that occurred while you were in the police department in Knin in August of 1990. And I think it's fair to say that you went to great lengths in your testimony to say that the break-in of -- the break-in to the police station in Knin was -- to get the reserve weapons was done by the citizens, by the people. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, before I ask you any more questions about the break-in to the police station, I want to ask you something else. The decision by the Croatian authorities to take control of the reserve police weapons in Knin, in Obrovac, in Benkovac, that was a lawful order, wasn't it? There was nothing illegal about that order or that decision, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that anybody opposing that order, taking steps to oppose the implementation of that order, would be breaking the law, would be violating a lawful order. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, are you -- are you aware that in April or May of 1990, the JNA took control of the Croatian Territorial Defence weapons? Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something from the media, from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to show you a document just to see if you can confirm its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's again that -- the report from Human Rights Watch from September of 1991, and the ERN again is 00276596, if we could have that up again. And if we could go to page 23 again, please. And could we go to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, again, I don't have a B/C/S of -- version of this, so I'll have to read it to you and it will be translated. In the last paragraph, the second sentence, it says -- and I'm just going to ask you after I read this if you can confirm its accuracy based on what you knew. "However, a few weeks before Slovenia and Croatia voted out their communist regimes in 1990, the Yugoslav army made efforts to confiscate weapons which were part of Slovenia's and Croatia's Territorial Defence units. In April 1990, just prior to the Croatian elections, the army confiscated most of the republic's weapons." Is that consistent with what you knew or heard at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it more or less. I don't know if that's the specific time period, but this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have an intervention. I don't know whether I would call it an objection, but it's about inconsistency as far as the time is concerned. In the previous remark, the Prosecutor said that the JNA confiscated the weapons in April, but here Human Rights Watch says that it was a few weeks before the vote on independence. I don't know what that means because the decision on independence was taken in 1991. Elections are one thing. This did take place in 1990, and they were multi-party elections, but the vote on independence, at least that's how I understood the question by the Prosecutor. We are now talking about a period of one year. I don't know whether those two questions are connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's find out. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I think Defence counsel is confused. The -- the sentence it says -- it is about April of 1990, and the sentence says: "A few weeks before Slovenia and Croatia voted out their communist regimes in 1990 ..." It's not about the independence declaration in 1991. It's about the multi-party elections in 1990. And then the second sentence is very specific. It says: "In April 1990, just prior to the Croatian elections, the army confiscated most of the republic's weapons." So I don't think there's any contradiction at all in the chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just to go back to your answer, sir, before that interruption, do I understand your answer to be that, yes, this happened. The only thing you're not absolutely sure about is the exact time it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to the so-called break-in of the -- I won't say "so-called." The break-in of the Knin public security station to -- in August of 1990, did you ever learn that in fact the break-in to seize the weapons was organised by Milan Martic and others and it was made to look like the citizens had done it? Did you learn that fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't learn that. That was something that was never indicated to me and I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I go on on this topic, I failed -- could I move into evidence the document that I was referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document -- the one on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document on the screen is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become exhibit number 895.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you never heard that before? Before today you never heard that, that Milan Martic had organised the break-in and made it look like -- Milan Martic and others, and made it look like the public had done it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to go again to the interview that Mr. Martic gave in October 1994. I'm going to rely on a transcript this time, and if we could go -- if we could have Exhibit 496, please. And in English -- if we could go on English to page 6 and also page 6 of the B/C/S, please. And just to -- as a word of explanation about this transcript. The questions -- the answers are recorded on this transcript but not the questions -- whenever there's a question, it simply says "question." The actual question is not recorded but the answer is transcribed. That's why this sort of confusing nature of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when I say "page 6," I mean page 6 on the e-court page 6. I can give the ERN. The ERN is 550 -- that's it. That's page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: 5509. Is that also in the -- I can't -- yeah, okay. Can we find -- would it be possible for the B/C/S, to shrink it down so we can see the whole page, please? Now -- and then focus in on the second half there where it says: "On the 17th of August ..." There we go. And if we could blow up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm just going to read there. On the -- this is Milan Martic speaking. "On the 17th of August, two days before our referendum, we got on info that Croatia with its police had started to disarm the police stations in Serbian opstinas. In Knin we allowed them to disarm us. In agreement with Raskovic and Babic, we decided to take all the weapons from the storages of the reserve militia and we made a false attempt as if the citizens broke into the storage. We took the arms and from that moment I personally assumed the command over the roadblocks." And then I'll go to the next answer, so if we could scroll down, please, on the B/C/S. He said: "I remember every detail when we agreed that I will be in charge of the feigned break-in to the police station to take the weapons and distribute them to the fighters. And I said to Dr. Babic: No problem, I'll do that, and you proclaim the state of emergency."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we have to turn to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then I'm going to jump down to the bottom of the page in English. "I went to the police station and" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in English. "... and ordered that they feign the break-in. We took the weapons and I left with the people and in Golubic distributed those weapons to the fighters. About 300 rifles, and I created a battalion apart from the regular police. Around 5.00 p.m. Dr. Babic proclaimed not the state of emergency but the state of war and this entered history as the proclamation of the state of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, having seen this account from Mr. Martic about those events, would you accept, sir, that even while you were at the police department in Knin you did not know everything that was happening. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this figure of 300 rifles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you know? It can't be probable that you knew. You either knew or you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if this is true, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the question. Did you know these things that are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, there's a reference to the distribution of weapons in Golubic on that day, and we've had other testimony in this trial about that. Were you aware, sir, that on the 17th of August, 1990, Milan Martic and others distributed weapons in Golubic to reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, reserve policemen had not been engaged by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you because that's an answer to a different question than the question I put to you. The question I put to you is: Did you know that Milan Martic distributed weapons to reserve policemen on August 17th, 1990? Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it to reserve police or is it to police apart from the regular police?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm -- Your Honour, I'm relying on evidence that's been given in this trial about that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, you're not relying on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I'll rephrase the question so that we don't have that difficulty, Your Honour. I think I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. Are you aware, sir, that on August 17th, 1990 Milan Martic distributed weapons in Golubic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So that's another thing you didn't know about. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you also did not know the people to whom these weapons were distributed were people other than regular police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. My men were not members of that section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you also testified in direct examination that you didn't think that the police had anything to do with the barricades from the time they appeared until January of 1991. Is that -- you recall -- is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you also told us, didn't you, that after August 1990 you in fact did not see Milan Martic around very much, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And we just saw in this transcript of this interview that Mr. Martic said that -- said: "I personally -- I personally assumed the command over the roadblocks." Did you see that in the interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember -- do you remember I read it out just a few minutes ago. Do you remember me reading it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think it's on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is on the previous page. Thank you, Your Honour. And it's 5509 in the English. You know, I'm not absolutely sure -- oh, yeah, I think it's the last sentence on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see, sir, where it says: "From that moment I personally assumed the command over the roadblocks." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And would you accept that that in fact was true and is simply something you did not know, another thing that you did not know about at the time? Would you accept that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it true, sir, that in fact members of the Serbian -- let me put this differently. Serb policemen appeared at -- helped man roadblocks in the Krajina in Knin municipality after in -- after August 17th, 1990? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It's not true as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if -- if I may, could we go back to your statement that you gave in the year 2000, and I believe you still have it before you. And I'd ask you to look at page 3 of the B/C/S, and it's page 3 of the English. And there's a paragraph that begins -- on the English it's the -- it's the third full paragraph, and the paragraph begins: "At the same time, the order from Zagreb was to lift barricades ..." And part way through that paragraph it says: "The police officers justified the existence of the barricades and supported the people's move." That's true, isn't it, sir? The police officers supported the barricade, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the police officers just said so in daily conversations, and that's what I meant when I -- when I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that Serb policemen did not stand by the barricades and manned them during 1990 that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not actively participate at the barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, if they were standing and manning the barricades alongside with locals, you would call that actively participating at the barricades, would you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would call that active participation, if they stood guard, stopped people in vehicles, checked papers, and performed other duties normally performed at barricades, then I would call it active participation. But to my knowledge none of them did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be something else that was happening; that is, police were engaging in these activities but you did not know about it? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I guess what I mean is that you did not -- you were in Knin. You did not observe all of the barricades around the Knin municipality, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's possible that police were participating in these ways and you simply did not know about it. Isn't that possible? You would accept that that's possible, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, too, is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at something else in your statement here. It's on page -- it's still on page 3, and it's at the top of the page in English. I can't tell you exactly where it is in the B/C/S. But the paragraph begins: "The tensions were growing ..." And this is a reference -- the time period is -- from the context is August of 1990. And then it -- do you see that paragraph that starts: "The tensions were growing. People were afraid, remembering mass slaughters"? Have you found that paragraph on page 3, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure you were with us. And then it says: "People were afraid, remembering mass slaughters of Serbs by Croats during the Second World War." And this is the sentence -- the two sentences that I'm interested in: "Those actions were orchestrated by a so-called Serb people's resistance. The seat of this organisation was in Knin." Now, that's a reference, is it not, to an organisation that's sometimes called the Council for National Resistance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say the names are similar, and their functions, duties, were the same, their purpose was the same. Resistance, council for resistance, would mean the same thing, something that was meant to offer resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this council came into existence after August 17th, 1990, and was -- one of its functions was to organise and coordinate the barricades, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible they did that. I was not familiar with the work and command there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say in that sentence: "Those actions were orchestrated by a so-called ..." What actions were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I was giving that statement in 2000, I was thinking of all those actions aimed at putting up the barricades, the roadblocks, and all the stories and rumours that circulated. That's what I had in mind when I was giving that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So by "those actions" you meant the barricades and the roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The shifts of personnel, food, everything that was possibly going around those barricades. The entire logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that Milan Martic was one of the commanders or one of the leading figures in the Council for National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you aware that he played a role, that he participated in the activities of the Council for National Resistance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no information to that effect or evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you didn't know that first he was based in this capacity in Golubic and then he moved shortly thereafter to the village of Oton, and then sometime later moved to - and I'm going to mispronounce this, I'm sure - Sinobadova Glavica? You weren't aware of that then, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document which is in evidence in our case. It's Exhibit 872. This is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a statement that was taken, you'll see here, on the 2nd of December, 1990, by the JNA security organs. And you'll see the name Zdravko Tolimir there on the left, perhaps a name that's familiar to you. Is that name familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the name of Zdravko Tolimir is familiar and Dragomir Pecanac is also familiar. I don't know the third person, Ognjen Biserko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the first page of the statement, please, and I'm just going to focus in on some parts and then ask you if this refreshes your recollection or if you know anything about what's being discussed in the statement. And from the English I'm going to start reading from the last sentences of the page, and you'll have to tell me, sir, if you see it. I think it's -- yes, I think it will be on this page. "I know that after the state of war was proclaimed," and that's a reference to the 17th of August, 1990, "village guards were organised and barricades set up in view of defence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not with you. I'm on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I see there's a different version in the -- it's -- on this version it's on the middle of the page of the English. "I'm aware that after a state of war was declared" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't realise I had a different version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "I also know that in Golubic village the staff for the defence of Knin was created, which was later named -- renamed the Council of National Resistance. I know this because radio and telephone communication links were maintained between this staff and the reporting centre. I don't know exactly in which way this staff was formed, but I do know which persons used its communications to call me. They were Milan Martic, inspector of the Knin SJS," and some other names are then listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then if we could turn to the next page in English, and I think we'll also have to turn to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A few lines down it says: "Martic said that he had been appointed Chief of Staff and that Milan Babic was the one who appointed them all to these functions in order to do the job seriously. I don't know for how long exactly this staff operated and controlled the organisation of resistance by inhabitants of Golubic village because it changed its location repeatedly being based in Oton village at a time and then in the memorial centre on Sinobadova Glavica in Knin. I know that after some time the Council of National Resistance, against violence inflicted on the Serbs, took over the functions of the staff. The Council was made up of Milan Martic, Milan Dragisic," and some other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you know anything about what is stated here in this statement or are these things that you were completely unaware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this statement I recognise several persons whom I know as citizens of Knin, but I know truly nothing about the events -- about the event concerned. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So again, would you accept that during this time period, August/September 1990, there were things happening in Knin municipality that you were not aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, would you accept that that in fact could be very possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible, possible. I said it was possible that this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, certainly you would agree with me, would you not, that by the time the so-called log revolution started in August of 1990, from then on the Croatian police had no real authority in Knin, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not agree with you for several reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me -- before I hear those reasons, let me put to you something -- some things that you said yourself in your direct examination. You told us that officers refused to implement several plans to withdraw the weapons from Knin. You told us also that around the 22nd of August officers in Drnis threw down their weapons and refused to implement an order that had come from Sibenik. And you told us that those officers thereafter weren't fired from their positions for refusing the order, that they in fact were allowed to transfer to whatever police department they wanted to go to. Don't those things indicate that the Croatian authorities had, if not no authority in Knin, had extremely diminished authority in Knin? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours and honourable Mr. Prosecutor, the entire life of all the people and the town of Knin was not reduced only to those barricades and their operation. In addition to barricades, we had traffic, there were thefts, embezzlements, car accidents, bar brawls, normal work was going on, registrations were to be issued, IDs, all the other work of the organs of internal affairs. We conducted our crime investigations, apprehended people, cooperated with the justice system. We investigated break-ins into rail cars transporting weapons. We reported to Zagreb, to Sibenik. We're doing many other things. Imagine -- imagine whether Zagreb, the MUP of Zagreb, and the state of Croatia would be paying us if they really thought we were not doing most of what our job normally consists of. So life was not just barricades. There was normal life going on elsewhere in the territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, I think --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think that's something you've told us now a number of times, and I think I understand your answer, though wouldn't you agree with me, sir, that on all those other matters, those are matters that the police in Knin were happy to cooperate with other police on, but that if they did not want to cooperate, then they wouldn't? For example, on the barricades. So ultimately it was up to the Serb police when they would cooperate and when they wouldn't. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it this way. Maybe they gave me wrong, false, information and then I forwarded that false information to superior commands, but I didn't have evidence of anything like that. I didn't have evidence that they held something back from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand, though the point of my question really was the -- and I'll put it -- I'll try to put it very simply. Croatian authorities had authority in Knin only to the extent that the Serb majority there agreed with that authority or agreed for them to have authority. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even that is not completely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it's right with respect to the barricades and the disorder that surrounded the barricades? On those topics, the Croatian authorities had no authority in Knin, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as barricades are concerned, I would agree that they had no power at all, no authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll move on. Let's talk about arming. You testified - and I'll quote you - that -- and this is from 6808, that "throughout August and September 1990, weapons were the main thing everyone was talking about and everybody was bending over backwards in order to get weapons." Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also talked, and this is at 6809, about various break-ins that occurred. You described a case -- two case -- cases where the train was broken into, and on one occasion ten rifles were taken and on another occasion five or six were taken. And you told us about World War II weapons that were surfacing and about weapons permits being forged. Do you remember all those topics, sir? You have to answer verbally, otherwise it doesn't get recorded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I spoke about that. I'm sorry, I hadn't realised that you were finished with your question, so I was waiting. And now I can confirm that I understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. Now, just -- just to be clear, you're talking about Serb civilians in Knin obtaining weapons by these various methods, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you also testified, and this is at 6812, that: "We couldn't take measures to confiscate all the weapons because that would pit us against the population." Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes there's an interruption. I lose the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Should I repeat my question because it wasn't -- there was an interruption?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified, and I'll quote, it's from 6812: "We couldn't take measures to confiscate all the weapons because that would pit us against the population." Do you remember that testimony in your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you testified also, and I'll quote you again, that: "We could not embark on the disarmament or disarming of those people manning the barricades because that would have led to a very difficult situation. I or any of my police officers or any of my superiors did not wish to disarm the people in that way." That's from 6812. Do you remember that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you don't believe, do you, that the Serbs in Knin armed themselves only by break-ins of trains and shops, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they obtained that in ways I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, wasn't there already at this time an organised effort to arm the Serbs and that weapons were arriving from Serbia, or is that something that you were not aware of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know of any organised action whereby weapons would arrive from Serbia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me just show you again Exhibit 872 and see if you are aware of anything that is discussed in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could look at page -- well, I -- from my version it's page 5 of the English. It's page 4 of the B/C/S. Actually, I think it's probably on page 4 of the English, but I believe it's page 5 of the B/C/S. Could we go to the prior page on the B/C/S, please, and go -- yes. It's that second paragraph there at the bottom. I apologise. Yes, now I think we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, it states: "Concerning illegal arming of citizens, I can say that it is widespread. I know that about 1300 guns and 400 pistols have been infiltrated into the Knin and Obrovac municipalities. I know that 600 guns have arrived in Strmica. I think it was between 15 October 1990 and 19 October 1990. They came from the Crvena Zastava factory based in Kragujevac," which is in Serbia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "Through the mediator RO Sport from Belgrade which runs a business in Knin." Did you know anything about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that transport of weapons and the quantity of weapons which arrived in the Knin area. I heard about it in 1991 and 1992 during the war, that Simo Dubajic was mentioned sold carbines for certain sums of money. I don't know whether the amount was 1.000 marks or something like that. But this is all the information. I never bought a carbine, and in this case, when we're talking about this event, when I see the dates and the quantities, that's all I know. Later during the war, I did hear stories that there were carbines passing in the territory, such shipments, and that they were being bought and sold. That's what I heard later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you heard that later during the war, was it in reference to events that had occurred in the fall; that is, September, October, November of 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I wasn't really paying attention to the time. There were many events. It's possible that it was related to this period, I mean carbines were probably not being brought in in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, can I -- let me try to put the question more directly to you. As you sit here today, do you recall hearing in 1991 that weapons had been brought in -- carbines had been brought in and sold during 1990? Do you recall hearing those stories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that the person mentioned in the statement, Mr. Simo Dubajic, sold carbines. I don't know how they reached Knin and what the quantity was or I don't know when exactly they arrived. But I heard that he was selling carbines and that the price was approximately 1.000 German marks. That was the counter value.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me just read a -- just a bit more from this statement. And it's at the bottom of page 4 in the English and it's going to be on the next page in the B/C/S. Towards -- more towards the top. Just making sure it's on -- yes, okay. It's about halfway down the screen in the B/C/S there. And it starts the last sentence on -- in the English version: "The same evening at about 1800" -- and the reference is to 16th November 1991, "Nanic told us at the centre that he had just driven in about 400 guns and 200 or 300 pistols of the type TT Duga Devetka, and he was supposed to transport them to the village of Krupa to give them to his godfather Simo Dubajic." And then it tells that he drove them from the manufacturer in Kragujevac. I'm sorry. Does that help you remember that these -- that these quantities, these kinds of weapons were being brought by various channels from Serbia at the time or do you still have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, sir, I cannot change all that I know in one minute. I have already said most of the things that I know, and I want to say as much here so that the truth can be determined. I was never present and I didn't have documents pertaining to this. This person, Simo Dubajic, is mentioned here in relation to Krupa, but I know that he actually comes from a place called Kistanje, not Krupa. When this statement was taken -- I mean, there is a lot of information here. I don't know whether it's all precise and correct. I'm not doubting the statement as a whole, but I'm sure that there are some details that are not so correct. Perhaps they are, but it's my information that I don't know that so many weapons came to the territory of Knin. As I said, all I know is that during the war in different meetings and through various events, I found out that these weapons were there. All I know is that the cost was 1.000 German marks. I don't know whether it was for one or two carbines. I am not somebody who is particularly interested or ever had any hunting weapons. All I had was my officially issued pistol. That's all that I had. I wasn't interested in anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear about the purpose of these questions, I'm interested only in what you know and what you do not know. It's only what you know. But also just to -- just -- you would agree with me that in the statement it does not say that Simo Dubajic comes from the village of Krupa, it's a reference that he's transporting weapons to Krupa, right? Isn't that what it says? ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-096 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Krupa, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I intervene, please? Can we all try to make sure that, at least when the witness is speaking, all other microphones are off. Apparently his voice can be heard outside the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've tried to remember to turn mine off, but I may have missed a few times. I'll take greater care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm also asking everybody else who is sitting around. Please make sure that the microphones are off. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting, now that my microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, I know it's about two minutes early, but I'm just going to go into another document which will require more time than two minutes. So perhaps we could break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are ever so grateful to you, Mr. Whiting. Thank you so much. We will now break for the day and reconvene tomorrow at quarter past -- at 9.00 in the morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of August, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.40 p.m.,
